slots.sample: Tracy Base is an example website studio bringing design, development and content together. Use these sample pages to introduce your own business, explain your services and help visitors take the next step.
slots.label: About us

slots.sample: Explore the type scale, heading hierarchy and readable body text used throughout the template.
slots.label: Typography

slots.sample: Body rhythm, heading scale, and muted metadata all resolve through the committed token contract.
slots.label: Typography

slots.sample: The preview intentionally uses only schema tokens so reviewers can confirm the package remains portable across OpenDesign artifacts.
slots.label: Typography

slots.sample: Start with the people your website needs to help. We turn audience questions, business priorities and existing content into a clear page plan.
slots.label: Website strategy

slots.sample: The first deliverable is a practical brief: who each page serves, what it needs to explain and the action a visitor should be able to take. Reviewing this together keeps design decisions tied to a shared purpose.
slots.label: Website strategy

slots.sample: A recognisable website needs more than a logo. Colour, typography, photography and interaction should feel like parts of the same business.
slots.label: Brand and interface design

slots.sample: We explore the key pages before extending the visual language across the site. This gives your team something concrete to review and leaves a small, useful set of design rules for future content.
slots.label: Brand and interface design

slots.sample: A good design should remain useful after launch. We build pages around editable sections so your team can keep services, people and news up to date.
slots.label: Website development

slots.sample: We review navigation, forms and layouts with realistic content on small and large screens. Handover includes a walk-through of the pages your team will change most often.
slots.label: Website development

slots.sample: Specific words and relevant images help people understand what you do. We plan content around customer questions and choose visuals that explain the work.
slots.label: Content and photography

slots.sample: The content plan identifies the message, image and next step for each section. Photographs should show the product, process or people behind the service; captions provide context rather than repeat the headline.
slots.label: Content and photography

slots.sample: Websites need attention as a business changes. A regular review helps keep contact information, services, software and the visitor journey current.
slots.label: Website care

slots.sample: Begin with a list of important pages and forms. Record what changed, check the result on a phone and keep a recovery point before technical updates. Agree who receives and follows up on enquiries.
slots.label: Website care

slots.sample: A useful brief explains the business problem before listing page features. Describe your audience, the questions they ask and what a successful visit looks like.
slots.label: Writing a useful website brief

slots.sample: Include existing pages, content owners and examples with a sentence explaining what you like about each. Separate essentials from ideas that can wait so the project has a clear first release.
slots.label: Writing a useful website brief

slots.sample: Someone arriving at a contact page is ready for a next step. Make the available channels and the information you need easy to understand.
slots.label: Designing a contact page people can use
Designing a contact page people can use

slots.sample: Keep required fields to a minimum. Explain what happens after submission and test where the message is delivered. An attractive form is only useful when a person can receive and respond to it.
slots.label: Designing a contact page people can use

slots.label: Testing a website before launch

slots.sample: Check links and forms with realistic text, including long names and messages. Review both appearance and delivery, and record who signs off each journey.
slots.label: Testing a website before launch

slots.sample: Moving a website changes more than its files. Existing URLs, media, search traffic and editorial habits all need a place in the plan.
slots.label: Planning a website migration

slots.sample: Inventory the current pages and map each important URL to its destination. Test redirects and forms on a preview, keep a recovery copy and schedule a review after the move.
slots.label: Planning a website migration

slots.sample: An image that works across a desktop banner may lose its subject in a phone crop. Choose the focal point before exporting the final sizes.
slots.label: Keeping images sharp on smaller screens
Keeping images sharp on smaller screens

slots.sample: Keep essential details away from the edges. Supply dimensions with the image, use an appropriate file size and check the actual crop beside its heading on a narrow screen.
slots.label: Keeping images sharp on smaller screens

slots.sample: Keeping images sharp on smaller screens
slots.label: Keeping images sharp on smaller screens

slots.sample: Maintenance becomes easier when each piece of content has a clear home. Repeated copy and unclear section names make routine edits harder than they need to be.
slots.label: Making a website easy to maintain
Making a website easy to maintain

slots.sample: Name sections by page and purpose, keep shared content in one place and write a short editing guide. Test the guide with someone who did not build the site.
slots.label: Making a website easy to maintain

slots.sample: Making a website easy to maintain
slots.label: Making a website easy to maintain

slots.sample: A website handover should give the owner confidence to make everyday changes. Access credentials alone do not explain how the site is organised.
slots.label: A practical handover checklist

slots.sample: Walk through changing a service, replacing a photograph and publishing a post. Record the support contact and recovery process, and confirm that the owner can complete those tasks.
slots.label: A practical handover checklist

slots.sample: A design review works best when everyone is responding to the same question. A focused session is more useful than a long list of unrelated preferences.
slots.label: Inside a collaborative design review

slots.sample: Share the goal and pages in advance. Discuss clarity, hierarchy and the next action, then record decisions in one place with a named owner for each follow-up.
slots.label: Inside a collaborative design review

slots.sample: Team photographs feel more natural when people know how the images will be used. Plan portraits, group scenes and working details as separate needs.
slots.label: Preparing for a team photo session
Preparing for a team photo session

slots.sample: Choose a consistent light and background for portraits. Leave room for different crops and ask for permission to use each image on the website and related materials.
slots.label: Preparing for a team photo session

slots.sample: Preparing for a team photo session
slots.label: Preparing for a team photo session

slots.sample: A workspace tells part of a studio’s story. Useful photographs show how people collaborate and what they make, rather than only furniture and decoration.
slots.label: A workspace that supports creative work
A workspace that supports creative work

slots.sample: Capture a mix of wide scenes and close details. Avoid displaying private client material on screens or printouts, and give each image a caption that explains its context.
slots.label: A workspace that supports creative work

slots.sample: A workspace that supports creative work
slots.label: A workspace that supports creative work

slots.sample: A workshop often produces more ideas than a first website release can contain. The next step is to turn those notes into a useful order.
slots.label: From workshop notes to a page plan
From workshop notes to a page plan

slots.sample: Group questions by audience need. Give each proposed page one main purpose, mark the content owner and identify what must be ready before design starts.
slots.label: From workshop notes to a page plan

slots.sample: From workshop notes to a page plan
slots.label: From workshop notes to a page plan

slots.sample: Clear copy helps people decide whether a service fits their needs. Start with the answer a visitor came for, then add enough detail to support it.
slots.label: Editing website copy for clarity

slots.sample: Replace broad promises with specific descriptions of the work. Read headings on their own: they should still explain the page’s structure and lead towards a useful next step.
slots.label: Editing website copy for clarity

slots.sample: A homepage introduces the business and helps visitors choose where to go. It does not need to contain every detail from every service.
slots.label: Choosing what belongs on the homepage
Choosing what belongs on the homepage

slots.sample: Prioritise the audience, offer, proof and next step. Link to deeper pages for process and scope, and remove sections that repeat the same message without adding evidence.
slots.label: Choosing what belongs on the homepage

slots.sample: Choosing what belongs on the homepage
slots.label: Choosing what belongs on the homepage

slots.sample: A small, sustainable editorial plan is more useful than an ambitious calendar nobody owns. Begin with questions customers already ask.
slots.label: Building an editorial calendar

slots.sample: Assign a purpose, owner and review date to each article. Balance practical guidance with business updates, and revisit older posts when services or processes change.
slots.label: Building an editorial calendar

slots.sample: A service name alone rarely tells a customer what they are buying. Explain the problem, the work involved and the outcome they can review.
slots.label: Making service pages more specific

slots.sample: Include scope, typical inputs and the next conversation. Be clear about what varies by project instead of promising one timeline or price for every situation.
slots.label: Making service pages more specific

slots.sample: Headings are a navigation system inside a page. They should tell a reader what the next section will help them understand.
slots.label: Writing headings that guide a reader
Writing headings that guide a reader

slots.sample: Use a clear hierarchy and descriptive language. Check how longer headings wrap on a phone and avoid relying on visual size alone to communicate their level.
slots.label: Writing headings that guide a reader

slots.sample: Writing headings that guide a reader
slots.label: Writing headings that guide a reader

slots.sample: A useful customer story explains the starting point, the work and what changed. Specific evidence is more convincing than a collection of superlatives.
slots.label: Using customer stories responsibly

slots.sample: Ask permission before publishing names, logos or quotes. Keep results in context and label illustrative examples so readers can distinguish them from verified customer work.
slots.label: Using customer stories responsibly

slots.sample: A review workflow should make it clear who checks accuracy, who approves wording and who publishes. Too many parallel copies make that harder.
slots.label: A simple content review workflow

slots.sample: Work from a single draft, collect comments in one place and record the approval. After publishing, check the live page and set a date to review time-sensitive details.
slots.label: A simple content review workflow

slots.sample: A campaign page works best when its offer and audience are specific. The headline, supporting detail and action should all serve that one purpose.
slots.label: Planning a focused campaign page

slots.sample: Match the promise in the campaign message to the landing page. Remove distracting detours, explain the next step and confirm that enquiries reach the right person.
slots.label: Planning a focused campaign page

slots.sample: A CMS decision should include the people who will maintain the website. The best fit depends on their everyday tasks as much as the feature list.
slots.label: Choosing a CMS your team can use
Choosing a CMS your team can use

slots.sample: Try representative edits before committing: change a service, replace an image and publish a post. Review permissions, support and the effort required to keep the platform current.
slots.label: Choosing a CMS your team can use

slots.sample: Choosing a CMS your team can use
slots.label: Choosing a CMS your team can use

slots.sample: Hosting supports the website’s availability, updates and recovery. Compare responsibilities and support arrangements alongside capacity and price.
slots.label: Asking better questions about hosting

slots.sample: Ask how backups are restored, who handles incidents and what access the owner receives. Keep a written record of the arrangement so responsibilities remain clear after launch.
slots.label: Asking better questions about hosting

slots.sample: An asset inventory connects every photograph, document and logo to its purpose. It helps a team spot missing materials before pages are built.
slots.label: Preparing an asset inventory

slots.sample: Record the owner, usage permission and intended page for each asset. Keep originals separate from web exports and use descriptive filenames that the next editor can recognise.
slots.label: Preparing an asset inventory

slots.sample: Each integration adds a dependency to the website. Map the data it receives and the task it serves before deciding whether to include it.
slots.label: Reviewing third-party integrations

slots.sample: Test failure states as well as successful requests. Identify who owns the external account, how access is managed and what the visitor sees when the service is unavailable.
slots.label: Reviewing third-party integrations

slots.sample: Website proposals become easier to compare when they describe the same scope. A headline price can hide different assumptions about content and support.
slots.label: Comparing proposals on the same basis
Comparing proposals on the same basis

slots.sample: Ask for deliverables, review rounds, responsibilities and handover details. Separate recurring costs from project work and clarify how changes to the brief will be handled.
slots.label: Comparing proposals on the same basis

slots.sample: Comparing proposals on the same basis
slots.label: Comparing proposals on the same basis

slots.sample: A recovery plan describes how a site gets back to a known working state. Keeping a backup is one step; testing its restoration is another.
slots.label: Making recovery part of launch planning
Making recovery part of launch planning

slots.sample: Record where copies are stored and who can restore them. Practise on an isolated environment and confirm that content, media and forms work after the restoration.
slots.label: Making recovery part of launch planning

slots.sample: Making recovery part of launch planning
slots.label: Making recovery part of launch planning

slots.sample: Updates are easier to manage when they follow a repeatable routine. A small checklist helps prevent the same important checks being forgotten.
slots.label: A routine for website updates

slots.sample: Take a recovery point, review changes on a preview and test key journeys. Record the version and result, then monitor the live site after the update.
slots.label: A routine for website updates

slots.sample: Forms are part of an operational process, not just page decoration. A message needs a destination and someone responsible for answering it.
slots.label: Keeping forms connected to your team
Keeping forms connected to your team

slots.sample: Send a test enquiry through each important form and confirm receipt. Check spam handling and response ownership, and repeat the test after changes to email services.
slots.label: Keeping forms connected to your team

slots.sample: Keeping forms connected to your team
slots.label: Keeping forms connected to your team

slots.sample: Analytics are useful when they answer a business question. A large report is less helpful than a small set of measures the team understands.
slots.label: Reading website analytics with a purpose
Reading website analytics with a purpose

slots.sample: Choose the journeys you want to improve and look for points where people stop. Combine the numbers with customer feedback before deciding what to change.
slots.label: Reading website analytics with a purpose

slots.sample: Reading website analytics with a purpose
slots.label: Reading website analytics with a purpose

slots.sample: Page weight often grows one small addition at a time. Images, fonts and optional widgets should each earn their place in the visitor experience.
slots.label: Reducing unnecessary page weight

slots.sample: Review the largest assets first and remove features that no longer serve a purpose. Check the result on a typical phone connection instead of relying only on a fast office network.
slots.label: Reducing unnecessary page weight

Studio notes: starting with the customer

slots.sample: Use your own update to explain one decision and how feedback informed it. A short account with a relevant image often tells readers more than a broad claim about creativity.

slots.label: Studio notes: making time for improvements
Studio notes: making time for improvements

slots.sample: Group examples by the problem they address and add a short note about what is useful. Keep references separate from finished brand assets so they are not mistaken for approved work.

slots.label: Keeping project decisions findable

slots.sample: Write down the question, the choice and its practical consequence. Link to the relevant page or design and update the note when the decision changes.
slots.label: Keeping project decisions findable
